theme: I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 30. It is a psalm of thanksgiving for being brought back from the edge of death. Notice how it moves from mourning to dancing.
settingTheScene: The title reads, “A Psalm of David. A Song at the dedication of the temple.” The “house” may refer to David’s own palace, or to the temple site. In 2 Samuel 24 David numbers the people and faces a plague, which ended at the site where the temple would be built. Whatever the occasion, it is a psalm of a man who has come near to death and been raised.
observation: “I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up and have not let my foes rejoice over me” (v. 1).
“O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me” (v. 2).
“O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit” (v. 3).
“For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (v. 5).
“As for me, I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved” (v. 6).
“You hid your face; I was dismayed” (v. 7).
“You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness” (v. 11).
“That my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!” (v. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm is a story of three stages: security, crisis, and rescue. In the first, David was prosperous and said, “I shall never be moved.” He felt safe. But the security was in his prosperity rather than in God. Then God hid his face, and David was dismayed. The sudden loss of the sense of God’s presence showed him how much he depended on God. Third, he cried out, and God healed him.

The lesson is that comfort can breed complacency. When all is well, we can forget that we depend on God. Crises remind us. This is not a sentimental thought. David learned it by a frightening experience.

Verse 5 is one of the best-loved lines in the Psalter: “His anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.” It does not deny that the night is real. It says that the night will end. In the Bible, God’s discipline is brief compared to his kindness. The pain of this world is not the last word.

The reversal in verse 11 is a beautiful image. “You have turned for me my mourning into dancing.” It is God who does the turning. The sackcloth is loosed, and gladness is the new clothing. This is the pattern of the gospel: death becomes life, mourning becomes dancing.

The psalm ends with a purpose. God has done all this “that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent.” Our deliverance is meant to lead to worship. Silence is not an option for the one who has been rescued. David resolves to give thanks “forever.”
connection: The movement from night to morning is the pattern of Easter. Jesus’ mourning disciples saw him alive on the third day (John 16:20-22; Luke 24). “Joy comes with the morning” echoes Mary at the tomb at dawn (John 20:1). Paul says, “For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). Revelation 21:4 promises that mourning will pass away.
application:
Reflect on whether prosperity has made you too comfortable. Ask God to keep you dependent.

If you are in a night of weeping, hold on to verse 5 as a promise.

Think about how God has turned mourning into dancing in your own story, and share it with someone.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that his anger is for a moment and his favor for a lifetime.
Tell him what mourning you want turned into dancing.
Give him praise for healing you.
